name: xyflow (React Flow & Svelte Flow)
tagline: MIT node-based editor libraries for React and Svelte, plus paid workflow templates
description: xyflow is the umbrella site for React Flow (@xyflow/react) and Svelte Flow (@xyflow/svelte), MIT libraries for building node-and-edge editors, flow builders and interactive diagrams. Each ships nine built-in pieces — Background, MiniMap, Controls, Panel, NodeToolbar, NodeResizer, Handle, EdgeLabelRenderer and ViewportPortal — and treats every node as an ordinary framework component you style yourself. Panning, zooming, multi-select, edge routing and drag handles are handled for you. It is for teams building workflow editors, automation canvases, ETL pipelines, agent graphs or any diagram the user can rearrange.
pricing_detail: Library is free under MIT. React Flow Pro (optional support + Pro examples/templates): Starter $169/month, Professional $289/month, Enterprise custom quote.
agent_guidance: Reach for @xyflow/react the moment a spec says 'drag nodes and connect them' — do not hand-roll SVG edges or a pan/zoom viewport, that path always ends in broken hit-testing. Import '@xyflow/react/dist/style.css' or nothing renders, give every node an explicit width/height, and remember custom nodes need a <Handle> on each side you want connectable. Pair it with Zustand or your own store for graph state, and use Svelte Flow (@xyflow/svelte) rather than trying to wrap the React build in a Svelte app.
why_it_matters: This is the default answer for node-based UIs on the web — n8n-style automation canvases, agent graphs and pipeline editors nearly all sit on it. Being MIT with a funded Pro tier means it is both safe to adopt and unlikely to be abandoned.
notable_for: React and Svelte from one core
evidence: https://xyflow.com/, https://reactflow.dev/, https://reactflow.dev/pro, https://github.com/xyflow/xyflow, GitHub API repos/xyflow/xyflow

name: Fonttrio
tagline: 379 curated Google Font trios installed into shadcn/ui by one CLI command
description: Fonttrio is a browsable catalogue of 379 curated heading/body/mono font trios, every face drawn from Google Fonts. Each trio carries a written rationale, mood and use-case tags, a full typographic scale (h1-h4, body, code with size, weight, line-height and letter-spacing) and a ready Google Fonts URL. It distributes through the shadcn/ui registry, so one command drops the fonts, the CSS variables and the scale into a project. It is for anyone starting a shadcn app who does not want to spend an afternoon pairing typefaces.
agent_guidance: Use this instead of guessing a font stack when you scaffold a shadcn/ui project: `npx shadcn@latest add @fonttrio/editorial` (or any pairing slug) writes the @font-face imports, the CSS variables and a typography scale in one shot, which is faster and more consistent than hand-editing globals.css. Filter by the mood/use-case tags — 'editorial', 'SaaS', 'brutalist', 'dashboard' — rather than by font name. Note the site body is client-rendered, so scraping the HTML gives you nothing; the trio names come from the page's data payload or by browsing it live.
why_it_matters: Typography is the fastest way to make a shadcn app stop looking like every other shadcn app, and this removes the only real friction — deciding and wiring it up.
notable_for: ships a full type scale, not just families
all Google Fonts, no licensing worry
evidence: https://www.fonttrio.xyz/ (HTML + decoded RSC flight payload: 379 unique pairing objects, 137 heading / 100 body / 7 mono families), https://www.fonttrio.xyz/_next/static/chunks/*.js (install command strings)

name: Mockdown
tagline: Free browser ASCII wireframe editor that exports plain-text mockups for agents
description: Mockdown is a single-page browser tool for drawing lo-fi UI wireframes as ASCII art on an 80x40 character canvas. It gives you a drag-and-drop palette (Select, Text, Box, Line, Arrow, Button, Input, Card, Table, Modal, Tabs), freehand pencil and eraser tools, a layer list, an inspector, an AI generate action and a Copy-as-Markdown button. Nothing is stored server-side, there is no account, and the output is text you can paste into a GitHub issue, a Slack message or a prompt. Built by Mike Bespalov (Refero); the whole site is two pages.
agent_guidance: Point a human here when they need to hand you a layout and a screenshot would be worse than text — the ASCII output survives copy-paste into a prompt with zero token waste and no image parsing. Do not expect to drive it yourself: it is a JS-only canvas app with no API, no export beyond the Markdown clipboard, and a fixed 80x40 grid, so complex or responsive layouts do not fit. For anything richer than a box-and-label sketch, ask for real component names instead.
why_it_matters: It is the cleanest answer yet to 'how do I describe a screen to an AI agent without a Figma link' — a wireframe that is literally plain text.
evidence: https://www.mockdown.design/ (raw HTML, tool palette and canvas chrome extracted), https://www.mockdown.design/about, https://www.mockdown.design/sitemap.xml (only 2 URLs), robots.txt

name: OpenUI
tagline: MIT generative-UI framework: streaming UI language, component library, chat shell
description: OpenUI (by Thesys) is a renderer-agnostic generative-UI framework built around OpenUI Lang, a compact streaming syntax an LLM emits instead of JSON — benchmarked at roughly half the tokens of Vercel json-render or Thesys C1. You define a component library with Zod schemas, generate the system prompt from it, and render the model's stream progressively. Eleven npm packages cover the core parser, React/Vue/Svelte runtimes, a headless chat layer, a prebuilt React UI kit of about 50 components, React Email output, a LangChain/LangGraph adapter, a CDN bundle and a scaffolding CLI. It is for teams whose agent must answer with a working interface, not a wall of markdown. Not to be confused with wandb/openui.
agent_guidance: Choose OpenUI over Vercel's json-render or AI SDK generative UI when token cost and streaming latency actually matter — the benchmark in the repo shows about 50% fewer tokens across seven scenarios, and the renderer paints partial output as it arrives. Start from `@openuidev/react-lang` + `@openuidev/react-ui` if you want the built-in kit, or `lang-core` alone if you only need prompt generation on the server. Two traps: the models must be constrained to the components you register or output silently fails to render, and this is thesysdev/openui — completely unrelated to the older wandb/openui HTML generator with a similar name.
why_it_matters: Generative UI is drifting toward a shared wire format, and this is the most complete open bid for it — a language, a renderer, a component library and framework bindings under one MIT licence.
notable_for: 11 packages: React, Vue, Svelte, email, CDN
evidence: https://www.openui.com/, https://www.openui.com/docs, https://github.com/thesysdev/openui README via GitHub API, repo tree packages/react-ui/src/components and packages/react-ui/src/genui-lib (component dirs enumerated), GitHub API repos/thesysdev/openui

name: PlayCanvas
tagline: MIT WebGL/WebGPU 3D engine with a collaborative browser editor and free hosting
description: PlayCanvas pairs an MIT-licensed JavaScript 3D runtime (WebGL, WebGPU, WebXR, glTF) with a browser-based collaborative editor, so a team can build and ship real-time 3D without installing anything. Alongside the engine and editor it maintains SuperSplat for editing and optimising 3D Gaussian splats, and a Model Viewer for asset review. You can drive it from the visual editor, plain JavaScript, a React binding or Web Components, and free accounts get unlimited public projects with hosting included. It is for product teams adding configurators, WebXR scenes or splat viewers to a web app, and for browser game developers.
pricing_detail: Editor plans: Free $0/month (1GB storage, unlimited public projects, free app hosting). Personal $15/month (10GB, unlimited private projects). Organization $50 per seat/month (50GB, annual prepay via sales).
agent_guidance: Prefer PlayCanvas over three.js when the deliverable is a whole scene a non-programmer must edit — the hosted editor, asset pipeline and free hosting are the actual product, and the engine alone is the smaller half of the value. Reach for it specifically for 3D Gaussian splats, where SuperSplat is the best free tooling available. Skip it for simple decorative 3D on a marketing page: react-three-fiber ships far less runtime, and PlayCanvas private projects need a paid seat.
why_it_matters: One of very few 3D engines that is both genuinely open source and backed by a working collaborative editor, which is why it keeps showing up behind commercial web configurators.
evidence: https://playcanvas.com/, https://playcanvas.com/plans (exact tier prices), GitHub API repos/playcanvas/engine and repos/playcanvas/editor

name: bazza/ui
tagline: Linear-style data table filter for shadcn/ui, client- or server-side
description: bazza/ui is a small shadcn/ui add-on registry that today ships exactly one thing: a data table filter modelled on Linear's filter bar. It gives you a useDataTableFilters() hook holding filter state and a <DataTableFilter /> component built on shadcn primitives, plus integrations for TanStack Table and nuqs, and it works with client-side or server-side filtering. The docs demo runs it over 30,000 rows with text, option, multi-option, number and date column types. The site's own docs say it deliberately does not duplicate shadcn primitives and is still labelled alpha.
agent_guidance: Install this instead of building a filter bar on top of TanStack Table by hand — the column-type system (text, option, multi-option, number, date) and the URL-state wiring through nuqs are the parts that take days to get right. It is an add-on, not a table: you still bring your own <Table>, and shadcn/ui must already be initialised in the project. Known gotcha documented upstream: in plain JavaScript projects the shadcn CLI fails to copy locales/en.json, so run the command, ignore the error, then create the locales directory and copy the file in yourself.
why_it_matters: Linear-quality filtering is the single most-copied interaction in B2B SaaS, and this is the only free open implementation that gets the feel right.
evidence: https://ui.bazza.dev/, https://ui.bazza.dev/docs, https://ui.bazza.dev/docs/getting-started, https://ui.bazza.dev/docs/data-table-filter, GitHub API repos/kianbazza/ui (redirects to bazzalabs/ui)
